Warm-blooded [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] of the class Aves, characterized by [[Feather|feathers]], toothless beaked jaws, hard-shelled eggs, a high metabolic rate, a four-chambered [[Heart|heart]], and a strong yet lightweight skeleton.

Birds live worldwide and range in size from the 5.5 cm (2.2 in) bee [[Hummingbird|hummingbird]] to the 2.8 m (9 ft 2 in) [[Common ostrich]]. There are over 11,000 living species in 44 orders; more than half are [[Passerine|passerine]], or perching, birds. Nearly all have wings, which are modified forelimbs, although flight has been lost in some groups, including ratites and [[Penguin|penguins]]. Their digestive and respiratory systems are uniquely adapted for flight. The study of birds is called ornithology.

Birds evolved from earlier theropods and are the only living [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]]; in the modern cladistic sense they are considered reptiles, and their closest living relatives are the crocodilians. They descend from primitive avialans such as [[Archaeopteryx]], which appeared in the Late [[Jurassic]]. Modern birds evolved in the Late [[Cretaceous]] and diversified dramatically around the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]] 66 million years ago.

Birds are social, communicating through visual signals, calls, and songs. Most species are socially monogamous, usually for one breeding season at a time. Eggs are usually laid in a nest and incubated by the parents, and most birds give extended parental care after hatching.

Birds supply eggs, meat, and feathers, and [[Guano|guano]] is harvested as fertilizer. About 120 to 130 species have become extinct through human activity since the 17th century, and about 1,200 are threatened. Birdwatching is an important part of ecotourism.

Use of methods or devices to prevent pregnancy; also called contraception or fertility control.

Birth control has been used since ancient times, but effective and safe methods became available only in the 20th century; the combined oral contraceptive pill was approved for use in 1960. Planning, making available, and using it is called [[Family planning|family planning]]. Some cultures limit or discourage access because they consider it morally, religiously, or politically undesirable.

Methods include barrier methods, hormonal methods, intrauterine devices (IUDs), sterilization, and behavioral methods. The most effective are vasectomy, tubal ligation, IUDs, and implants, each with first-year failure rates of less than 1%. Hormonal pills, patches, vaginal rings, and injections follow; [[Condom|condoms]], diaphragms, and fertility awareness methods are less effective, and spermicides and withdrawal least. With typical use, first-year failure rates for hormonal pills, patches, and rings are 9%, owing to inconsistent use. [[Sterilization (medicine)|Sterilization]] is not usually reversible; other methods are. Condoms also help prevent [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]]. Emergency birth control can prevent pregnancy if taken within 72 to 120 hours after unprotected sex.

All methods carry some potential adverse effects, but the risk is less than that of pregnancy. Hormonal methods are associated with a 2- to 4-fold increased risk of venous thromboembolism and with elevated breast cancer incidence during use.

Comprehensive [[Sex education|sex education]] and access to birth control reduce unintended pregnancies among teenagers. About 222 million women in developing countries who want to avoid pregnancy are not using a modern method. In developing countries, birth control has decreased pregnancy-related deaths by 40% (about 270,000 deaths prevented in 2008). Some commentators link high contraceptive use in developed nations to sustained sub-replacement fertility and aging populations.

Plague pandemic that struck Europe, the Near East, and [[North Africa]] from 1346 to 1353.

The Black Death was one of the most fatal pandemics in human history. Estimates of the dead range from up to 50 million to 75 to 200 million worldwide, including around 30% to 60% of the European population and approximately 33% of the Middle Eastern population. The disease was caused by the bacterium [[Yersinia pestis]], spread mainly by flea bites and also by contact with infected tissues or fluids and, in pneumonic cases, by respiratory droplets. Untreated bubonic cases had a mortality rate approaching 90 percent. Some researchers argue that human lice contributed significantly to the spread, challenging the rodent-centered account.

Its origin is disputed; one account places it in [[Central Asia]]. The plague reached Europe in 1347 on Genoese trading ships from the [[Crimea|Crimean]] port of Kaffa, spreading through Mediterranean ports including [[Sicily]] and [[Marseille]]. It is tentatively considered the second plague pandemic. The first, the plague of [[Justinian I|Justinian]], lasted from 541 to 549, with recurrences until 750, and was confirmed in 2013 as caused by *Y. pestis*.

Contemporary writers called the event the pestilence or the great death in English, and magna mortalitas in Latin. The name black death was not applied to this pandemic in English until the 1750s, with the term first attested in 1755 as a translation of the Danish *den sorte død*.

The pandemic was the second great natural disaster to strike Europe in the late Middle Ages, after the Great Famine of 1315–1317. It had far-reaching population, economic, and cultural effects: it disrupted feudal structures, raised wages for survivors, and prompted shifts in labor, religion, and medicine, including early quarantine measures and flagellant movements. Further outbreaks followed, and the European population did not regain its 14th-century level until the 16th century.

Astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping.

[[Albert Einstein]]'s theory of [[General relativity|general relativity]], which describes gravitation as the curvature of [[Spacetime|spacetime]], predicts that any sufficiently compact mass will form a black hole. The boundary of no escape is the [[Event horizon|event horizon]]; crossing it traps an object but produces no locally detectable change. General relativity also predicts a central singularity, where the curvature of spacetime is infinite.

The idea of a body from which light could not escape was proposed in the late 18th century by John Michell, whose letter of 1784 considered a star of the same density but 500 times the radius of the Sun, and independently by Pierre-Simon Laplace in 1796. In 1916, shortly after Einstein published the field equations, Karl Schwarzschild found the first solution describing a black hole. Many early 20th-century physicists were skeptical of such objects, and they were long considered a mathematical curiosity. Theoretical work in the 1960s showed they were a generic prediction of general relativity. The first widely accepted black hole was [[Cygnus X-1]], proposed as a black hole binary through studies between 1971 and 1974.

Black holes typically form when massive stars collapse at the end of their life cycle, often in a supernova, and can grow by absorbing surrounding mass. Stellar-mass black holes are typically a few to hundreds of times the Sun's mass. Supermassive black holes of millions to billions of solar masses exist at the centers of most galaxies; the radio source [[Sagittarius A*]] in the Milky Way contains one of about 4.3 million solar masses.

Black holes are detected through their effects on nearby matter and light. Infalling plasma forms a glowing accretion disk, which in extreme cases powers a quasar. Merging black holes emit gravitational waves, and the Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadows of M87* in 2019 and Sagittarius A* in 2022. Quantum field theory in curved spacetime predicts that event horizons emit [[Hawking radiation]], causing very slow mass loss.

Specialized connective tissue and body fluid of the circulatory system in humans and other vertebrates, delivering nutrients and oxygen to cells and carrying metabolic waste away from them.

Blood is composed of blood cells suspended in plasma. Plasma makes up about 55% of blood, is straw-yellow, and is 92% water by volume, with proteins, glucose, mineral ions, and hormones making up the rest. By volume, red blood cells account for about 45% of whole blood and white cells about 0.7%. In humans, blood accounts for about 7% of body weight, with an average adult volume of roughly 5 litres (11 US pt).

The most abundant cells are red blood cells (erythrocytes), numbering 4.7 to 6.1 million per microliter in men and 4.2 to 5.4 million in women. They contain [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]], which binds oxygen reversibly and transports it; mature mammalian red cells lack a nucleus and organelles. White blood cells (leukocytes), numbering 4,000–11,000 per microliter, are part of the [[Immune system|immune system]], destroying aberrant cells and attacking pathogens. Platelets (thrombocytes), numbering 200,000–500,000 per microliter, take part in clotting. The cancer of leukocytes is called [[Leukemia|leukemia]].

Blood pH is regulated within a narrow range of 7.35 to 7.45, and a pH below 6.9 or above 7.8 is usually lethal. The respiratory and urinary systems exert principal control over this acid–base balance.

Blood is pumped through the vessels by the [[Heart|heart]]. Arterial blood carries oxygen from inhaled air to the tissues, and venous blood carries carbon dioxide to the [[Lung|lungs]] to be exhaled. Blood is bright red when its hemoglobin is oxygenated and dark red when deoxygenated. Its other functions include supplying nutrients, removing waste such as urea and lactic acid, detecting foreign material through antibodies, clotting after vessel injury, transporting hormones, and regulating core body temperature.

Human blood is classified into the ABO groups (A, B, AB, O) and Rh factor (positive or negative), which matter for safe transfusions. Medical terms relating to blood often begin with hemo- or hemato-, from the Greek *haima*.

Tabletop game played with small pieces placed and moved in particular ways on a specially designed patterned board, sometimes with other components such as [[Dice|dice]].

The earliest known uses of the term board game date from the 1840s and 1850s. Card games that do not use a standard deck, and games using neither cards nor a board, are often loosely included under the labels table and board games or tabletop games.

Board games have been found at archaeological sites in many cultures. As of 2024, 14 sites reported 51 game boards from the [[Neolithic]] period, dating from the early 7000s BC to the mid-6000s BC, though caution has been urged against treating these as the earliest game playing. Senet, from ancient Egypt, has been argued to be the oldest known board game, with possible board fragments c. 3100 BC; its rules were never written down and are not decisively known. The Royal Game of Ur originated around 2500 BC in [[Mesopotamia]], and its rules survive on a cuneiform tablet written by a Babylonian astronomer in c. 177 BC–c. 176 BC. A set from Shahr-i Sokhta in Iran, with 27 pieces and 4 dice, dates to 2600–2400 BC. [[Mancala]] is a broad family of games of uncertain age found across Africa, the Middle East, and southern Asia. In Europe, Homer's *Iliad* mentions petteia, which later evolved into the Roman *ludus latrunculorum*. Patolli originated in Mesoamerica and was played by cultures including the [[Aztecs]].

The 1880s–1920s, called the Golden Age by American art historian Margaret Hofer, saw mass production make games cheaper and more available. [[Monopoly (game)|Monopoly]] (1935) was the most popular, with 500 million games played as of 1999. In the late 1990s companies began producing more new games, and *The Settlers of Catan* (1995) is often credited with popularizing German-style games outside Europe. A new Board Game Renaissance in the early 21st century included *Carcassonne* (2000) and *Ticket to Ride* (2004).

Games vary in their balance of skill and luck: [[Chess|chess]] depends entirely on player skill, while children's games such as *Candy Land* (1949) and snakes and ladders are decided purely by luck.

Rigid organ forming part of the skeleton of most vertebrate animals.

Bones protect the organs of the body, produce red and white blood cells, store minerals, help regulate acid–base homeostasis, provide structure and support, and enable mobility and [[Hearing|hearing]]. They come in a variety of shapes and sizes and have complex internal and external structures. In the human body about 300 bones are present at birth; many fuse during development, leaving 206 separate bones in the adult, not counting numerous small sesamoid bones. The largest is the femur, or thigh bone, and the smallest is the stapes in the middle ear.

Bone tissue is a mineralized [[Connective tissue|connective tissue]] with an intercellular honeycomb-like matrix. Its organic component is mainly ossein, a form of collagen, and its inorganic component is bone mineral, made of various salts, chiefly calcium phosphate. Osteoblasts form bone, osteocytes mineralize it, and osteoclasts resorb it. Bone tissue comprises dense cortical (compact) bone and porous cancellous (spongy) bone, and bones may also contain marrow, periosteum, nerves, blood vessels, and [[Cartilage|cartilage]]. Bone is remodeled throughout life in response to mechanical stress.

Five types are found in the human body: long, short, flat, irregular, and sesamoid. Long bones, such as most limb bones, have a shaft called the diaphysis and a rounded epiphysis at each end. Short bones, such as those of the wrist and ankle, are roughly cube-shaped. Flat bones, such as most skull bones and the sternum, are thin and curved. Sesamoid bones, such as the patella, are embedded in tendons and increase the leverage of muscles. Irregular bones include the vertebrae and pelvis.

Mechanically, bone has a high compressive strength of about 170 MPa, a poorer tensile strength of 104–121 MPa, and a very low shear strength of 51.6 MPa. It is essentially brittle but has significant elasticity, contributed chiefly by collagen. The bones of the [[Skeleton|skeleton]] support the body, anchor muscles and tendons, and protect organs, as the [[Skull|skull]] protects the brain. Bone also acts as a reservoir of calcium and phosphate, houses bone marrow, and, through osteocalcin, functions as an endocrine organ.

Written work of substantial length, typically printed pages bound together and protected by a cover.

Books are broadly classified into [[Fiction|fiction]], containing invented or imaginary narratives, and non-fiction, containing content intended as factual truth. They may also appear as audiobooks and electronic books. Google Books estimated in 2010 that roughly 130 million unique books had been published. The word comes from the Old English *bōc*, possibly from a Germanic root meaning beech; the Latin *codex*, the format of the modern book, originally meant block of wood.

There is no consensus on a basic definition. [[UNESCO]] defined a book in 1964, for national statistics, as a non-periodical printed publication of at least 49 pages, exclusive of the cover pages, published in the country and made available to the public. Historian James Raven proposed a broader definition: a portable, durable, replicable, and legible means of recording and disseminating information, which would include ebooks and the knot-based Andean quipu.

Proto-writing was independently developed into full writing in at least three cases: Sumerian [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] in [[Mesopotamia]], written Chinese, and the [[Maya script]] in Mesoamerica. The earliest surviving texts widely accepted as writing are cuneiform clay tablets, created c. 3200 BC during the Uruk period in modern Iraq. Librarian Fred Kilgour identified clay tablets, papyrus scrolls, the codex, printing, steam power, offset printing, and electronic books as the most significant technological changes. The codex, a bound book of separate leaves, arose in the Roman period around the 1st to 4th centuries AD and, unlike a scroll, allowed random access to content.

The invention of movable-type printing by [[Johannes Gutenberg]] c. 1440 accelerated production and lowered costs; before then, books were copied by hand, limiting access to elites and monasteries. The publishing process, now usually undertaken by commercial companies, has been reshaped by ebooks and audiobooks, and by accessible formats such as [[Braille|braille]] and large print. Books are sold in retail stores and online and borrowed from libraries. Their reception has had social consequences, including [[Censorship|censorship]] and, in periods of ideological conflict, destruction.

Branch of biology that studies the growth, reproduction, and evolution of plants; also called plant science.

Plants can be studied at levels from biochemistry, molecular biology, and genetics to ecology, pathology, anatomy, morphology, and taxonomy. Plants are defined in several ways; they include approximately 410,000 species of land plants, some 391,000 species of vascular plants, of which approximately 369,000 are flowering plants and approximately 20,000 are bryophytes. Traditionally, botany has also included the study of fungi and algae. The term comes from the Ancient Greek *botanē*, meaning pasture, herbs, or fodder.

Botany originated in prehistoric herbalism, the identification of edible, poisonous, and medicinal plants. Early botanical works have been found in ancient texts from India dating to before 1100 BC, from Egypt, and from China. [[Aristotle]]'s student Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC), called the Father of Botany, wrote *Enquiry into Plants* and *On the Causes of Plants*, the most important contributions to the subject until the Middle Ages. Pedanius Dioscorides wrote *De materia medica*, which was widely read for more than 1,500 years. Medieval physic gardens attached to monasteries were forerunners of university botanical gardens; the Padua garden of 1545 is usually considered the first still in its original location, and the first in England was the University of Oxford Botanic Garden in 1621. Cataloguing garden collections led in 1753 to the binomial nomenclature of [[Carl Linnaeus]], still used to name all biological species.

In the 19th and 20th centuries, new techniques included electron microscopy, analysis of chromosome number, and study of enzymes and other proteins. In the last two decades of the 20th century, botanists used molecular genetic analysis, including DNA sequences, to classify plants more accurately. Dominant 21st-century themes are molecular genetics and epigenetics, which study the control of gene expression during differentiation of plant cells and tissues.

Botanical research supplies staple foods, timber, oil, rubber, fibre, and drugs, such as aspirin derived from willow bark, and serves horticulture, agriculture, forestry, plant breeding, and the maintenance of biodiversity. An estimated 45% of known plant species face extinction risks (as of 2023).

Organ forming the center of the nervous system in all vertebrate and most invertebrate animals, consisting of nervous tissue and typically located in the head.

The brain receives information from the sensory nervous system, processes it (thought, [[Cognition|cognition]], and intelligence), and coordinates motor control and the [[Endocrine system|endocrine system]]. It acts on the body by generating patterns of muscle activity and by driving the secretion of hormones, allowing rapid and coordinated responses to the environment. Simple responses such as reflexes can be mediated by the spinal cord, but sophisticated control of behavior requires a centralized brain. Brains evolved independently in several bilaterian lineages, including arthropods, mollusks, and vertebrates.

Invertebrate brains arise from paired segmental ganglia of the ventral nerve cord. Vertebrate brains develop from the dorsal nerve cord as an enlargement at the end of the neural tube and can be embryonically divided into forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain. Together, the brain and [[Spinal cord|spinal cord]] constitute the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]]. In humans, the main regions are the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem. The cerebrum, the largest, has two hemispheres and four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital.

Brains are composed primarily of [[Neuron|neurons]] and glial cells. Glial cells provide structural and metabolic support, insulation, and guidance of development. Neurons send signals to specific target cells, sometimes over long distances, by means of axons, which are usually myelinated and carry rapid electrical pulses called action potentials. Each neuron connects by synapses to several thousand others. The human cerebral cortex contains approximately 14–16 billion neurons and the cerebellum an estimated 55–70 billion; another account gives about 86 billion neurons and 85 billion non-neuronal cells in total. The human brain weighs about 1.4 kg (3 lb) and consumes roughly 20% of the body's oxygen and energy while making up about 2% of body mass. Its capacity for neuroplasticity enables learning and recovery from injury.

The operations of individual brain cells are understood in considerable detail, but how they cooperate in ensembles of millions is unsolved. Modern neuroscience often treats the brain as a biological computer.
